query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy, exposure to elevated temperatures in oxidizing environments promotes the preferential oxidation of Ti at grain boundaries. This results in the formation of a discontinuous, brittle, Ti-rich oxide scale that easily spalls, thereby allowing oxygen to ingress along the grain boundaries and locally embrittle the fcc matrix. This localized embrittlement under oxidizing conditions ultimately governs accelerated degradation and can trigger catastrophic failure, whereas a reducing gas environment suppresses such oxide formation and its adverse effects.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous, single-phase fcc solid solution and minimal preexisting oxide on its surfaces and grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Switch the testing atmosphere from a high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing) environment to a reducing gas environment (for example, a controlled H2/N2 mixture) during elevated-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Expose samples at a service-relevant elevated temperature (e.g., around 800°C) for a defined duration under two different gas atmospheres: one with a high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing conditions) and one with a controlled reducing environment. All other factors such as pressure and exposure time are held constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and integrity of a discontinuous, Ti-rich oxide layer along the grain boundaries of the fcc microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, the Ti in the alloy preferentially oxidizes at the grain boundaries, forming a brittle oxide scale that fails to adhere, thereby opening fast diffusion paths for further oxygen ingress. This leads to local depletion of ductile matrix and embrittlement, which promotes catastrophic failure. In a reducing environment, the formation of this deleterious oxide is suppressed, maintaining better intergranular cohesion and overall mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: When the environment is switched from oxidizing to reducing at the same temperature, the primary measured property—mechanical integrity (e.g., ductility and resistance to brittle fracture)—will be improved relative to the baseline. Specifically, under reducing conditions, the oxide layer will be thinner or more adherent, with less evidence of grain-boundary embrittlement, delaying or preventing catastrophic failure.
generation.baseline: Exposure of the alloy at elevated temperature (around 800°C) under a high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing) environment.
generation.boundary: Findings apply under conditions typical of elevated-temperature service (e.g., around 800°C) and within controlled gas atmosphere partial pressures that distinctly represent oxidizing versus reducing environments.
generation.uncertainty: The exact roles and possible synergistic effects of the other alloying elements (such as Al and Cr) in oxide scale formation and their influence on adhesion and subsequent degradation are not fully certain. Their contributions may modify the kinetics or morphology of the oxide, potentially affecting the overall degradation mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy and conduct elevated-temperature exposures (e.g., 800°C for a fixed time) under two gas atmospheres: one oxidizing (high O2 partial pressure) and one reducing (using a H2/N2 gas mixture). After exposure, use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to characterize the oxide layer’s thickness, composition, and continuity along grain boundaries, and perform mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or fracture tests) to assess ductility and failure mode.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology at grain boundaries (via TEM)
Chemical composition mapping of the oxide (via EDS)
Mechanical property evaluation (ductility, fracture toughness, failure mode)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If exposure under reducing conditions does not produce a significantly thinner or more adherent oxide scale and does not result in measurably improved mechanical integrity (i.e. similar ductility and failure behavior as under oxidizing conditions), then the hypothesis that Ti-driven grain-boundary oxidation governs degradation and catastrophic failure will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Al seems to have a minor effect on both Ni and Co, both of which are the weakest oxidizing component and it seems to have no effects on both unoxidized and oxidized states. We infer that Al addition does not have significant electronic interaction with Co and Ni (Fig. 4h, i), this is shown as their oxidation behavior remains the same in Fig. 4d. Figure 4j summarizes these interactions where Mn-Al tends to have the strongest interaction and both Ni and Co being the weakest. This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition.
